verdict.rationale: The Bible supplies one return-vocabulary: 'coming or arrival' (parousia), 'unveiling or revealing' (apokalypsis), and 'visible appearing' (epiphaneia), all tied to a single visible bodily coming with a loud trumpet, descent on clouds, and gathering of the chosen ones (Matthew 24:29-31, 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, 2 Thessalonians 2:1, 1 Corinthians 15:52, Titus 2:13). On this footing the post-tribulation reading (the view that the gathering happens after the great tribulation) has strong unified lexical evidence, and the word 'after' (meta) in Matthew 24:29 is explicit. But three lexical realities prevent closure. First, the verb 'snatch or seize' (harpazo, Strong's G0726) carries both a sudden divine removal sense (Acts 8:39, 2 Corinthians 12:2, Revelation 12:5) and a forcible seizure sense (John 10:12, Matthew 11:12), and 1 Thessalonians 4:17 carries no temporal marker (a word fixing when something happens) pinning the snatching relative to the 'tribulation or pressure' (thlipsis). Second, the construction 'keep' (tereo) plus 'out of or from' (ek) in Revelation 3:10 lexically matches the same construction in John 17:15 where ek means kept while in, not removed from, so the preposition does not settle the matter. Third, the noun 'assembly or church' (ekklesia, Strong's G1577) is dense in Revelation chapters 1 to 3 and reappears only at 22:16, leaving Revelation 4 to 19 silent on the term, which one reading lens treats as a removal and another as a shift in referent. The pattern is materially contested.

scripture.force: The phrase 'immediately after the tribulation of those days' (Eutheos meta ten thlipsin ton hemeron ekeinon) places the cosmic darkening and the following appearing of the Son of Man on an explicit timeline after the 'tribulation' (thlipsis). The temporal preposition 'after' (meta) with the accusative (the direct-object grammatical form) articular noun (a noun carrying 'the') is unambiguously sequential and is the load-bearing term for the post-tribulation (after-the-tribulation) reading.

The Son of Man comes 'coming on the clouds of heaven' (erchomenon epi ton nephelon tou ouranou) with power and great glory, and 'all the tribes of the earth' (pasai hai phylai tes ges) see Him. This is overt and public, audible and visual language, not secret. The pairing of 'cloud' (nephele) plus 'come' (erchomai) matches Daniel 7:13 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, abbreviated LXX) vocabulary.

He sends His angels with a great trumpet, 'with a great trumpet' (meta salpingos megales), and they gather the chosen ones, 'they will gather together His chosen ones' (episynaxousin tous eklektous autou), from the four winds, 'from the ends of the heavens' (ap akron ouranon). The 'trumpet' (salpinx) plus chosen-ones-gathering vocabulary overlaps directly with 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 (salpinx, the dead in Christ, the living caught up), supporting one event.

The Lord Himself descends from heaven 'with a command shout' (en keleusmati), 'with an archangel's voice' (en phone archangelou), 'with the trumpet of God' (en salpingi theou). Every element, command shout, archangel voice, trumpet of God, is loud and audible. The vocabulary names a public 'theophany' (a visible manifestation of God), not a hidden removal, and the 'trumpet' (salpinx) aligns with Matthew 24:31 and 1 Corinthians 15:52.

'The surviving living' (Hoi zontes hoi perileipomenoi) 'will be caught up' (harpagesometha, the future passive of the verb 'snatch or seize' harpazo) together with the risen sleepers 'in clouds to meet the Lord in the air' (en nephelais eis apantesin tou kyriou eis aera). The verb 'snatch or seize' (harpazo), across its 14 occurrences in the Bible, means a sudden seizing, used for both divine removal (Acts 8:39, 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, Revelation 12:5) and forcible human action (John 10:12, Matthew 11:12, Matthew 13:19). The verb itself carries no temporal marker (a word fixing when something happens) pinning the snatching before, during, or after the 'tribulation' (thlipsis), so by lexicon alone the sequencing question is undetermined.

Paul binds the 'coming or arrival' (parousia) of the Lord and our 'gathering together' (episynagoge) 'to Him' (ep auton) under one preposition 'concerning' (hyper) and one article 'the', the related-root noun to the verb 'they will gather together' (episynaxousin) in Matthew 24:31. The grammar treats the coming and the gathering as one subject, weighing against a chronological gap between them.

'Unless the falling-away comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed' (Ean me elthe he apostasia proton kai apokalyphthe ho anthropos tes anomias). The adverb 'first' (proton) orders the 'falling-away' (apostasia) and revealing before the Day of the Lord. The Thessalonians evidently could be shaken thinking the Day had come, which presupposes they expected to still be present for events tied to it, complicating any framework that removes the church before these signs.

'Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed' (Mysterion lego, pantes ou koimethesometha, pantes de allagesometha). The 'change' (allasso) plus 'sleep' (koimaomai) pair matches 1 Thessalonians 4 (dead in Christ rise, living caught up) and is dated 'at the last trumpet' (en te eschate salpingi). The wording locates the change at the last 'trumpet' (salpinx), the same word as Matthew 24:31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

'In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet' (En atomo, en rhipe ophthalmou, en te eschate salpingi). The phrase 'last trumpet' (eschate salpinx) is a definite ordinal (a numbered position-word) that places the change at the final trumpet of a known series. Post-tribulation (after-the-tribulation) reading takes this as the same trumpet as Matthew 24:31; pre-tribulation (before-the-tribulation) reading treats it as a different last trumpet of a separate church-age sequence. The lexicon supplies one 'trumpet' (salpinx) vocabulary that does not differentiate which series is in view.

'I will keep you out of the hour of trial' (Tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou). The construction 'keep' (tereo) plus 'out of or from' (ek) occurs in only one other place in the Bible, John 17:15, where Jesus prays the opposite of removal, 'that you keep them out of the evil one' (hina teres autous ek tou ponerou), in a context that explicitly disclaims taking them out of the world ('not... that you take them out of the world,' ouk... aras autous ek tou kosmou). The same lexical construction in the Bible means kept while in, not extracted from, in its only parallel. The preposition 'out of or from' (ek) lexically allows both senses, motion-from and separation-from-within, and context here is contested.

John sees 'the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God' (psychai ton pepelekismenon dia ten martyrian Iesou kai dia ton logon tou theou), and 'those who did not worship the beast' (hoitines ou prosekynesan to therion). 'Beheaded with an axe' (pelekizo) is a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible. Lexically, these are saints who refused the beast and his mark, which requires them to have been on earth during the beast and his mark era. They then live and reign with Christ.

'I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them out of the evil one' (Ouk eroto hina ares autous ek tou kosmou, all hina teres autous ek tou ponerou). The verse uses the same 'keep' (tereo) plus 'out of or from' (ek) construction as Revelation 3:10 and explicitly contrasts removal ('take out,' airo ek) with preservation ('keep out,' tereo ek). It is the Bible's controlling parallel for the construction and shows that 'out of or from' (ek) does not entail spatial extraction.

'Relief with us at the revealing of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of His power' (Anesin meth hemon en te apokalypsei tou kyriou Iesou ap ouranou met angelon dynameos autou). Paul promises 'the ones currently being afflicted' (thlibomenoi) their relief AT (in, en) the 'unveiling or revealing' (apokalypsis) of the Lord from heaven with the angels of His power, not before it. The temporal 'at' (en) links rest for the afflicted directly to the public 'unveiling or revealing' (apokalypsis), the same vocabulary used elsewhere for the visible return.

'Awaiting the blessed hope and visible appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Prosdechomenoi ten makarian elpida kai epiphaneian tes doxes tou megalou theou kai soteros hemon Iesou Christou). The blessed hope is named as one event, 'the visible appearing of the glory' (epiphaneia tes doxes), joining hope and glorious appearing under one article 'the'. Lexically the 'visible appearing' (epiphaneia) vocabulary always denotes visible manifestation, not a hidden phase.

'At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ' (En te parousia tou kyriou hemon Iesou Christou). Paul uses 'coming or arrival' (parousia) again to date sanctification's completion, alongside its prior uses in 1 Thessalonians 2:19, 3:13, 4:15. Across all four chapters 'coming or arrival' (parousia) is a single referent, never differentiated into phases, so the vocabulary does not itself encode a two-stage coming.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'We shall be caught up' (Harpagesometha) asserts a sudden catching up but is temporally silent (does not say when). The verb 'snatch or seize' (harpazo) carries multiple senses across the Bible, covering both divine rescue (Acts 8:39, 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, Revelation 12:5) and forcible seizure (John 10:12, Matthew 11:12), and 1 Thessalonians 4:17 supplies no temporal adverb (a word fixing when) relative to the 'tribulation' (thlipsis). A separate prior removal reading treats the snatching as a distinct earlier event; a unified reading folds it into the visible appearing. The word-form alone cannot adjudicate; the question remains lexically unresolved at the level of the word.

'I will keep you out of the hour of trial' (Tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou) is the strongest single verse for a prior removal in the pre-tribulation (before-the-tribulation) reading, but the construction 'keep' (tereo) plus 'out of or from' (ek) occurs identically in John 17:15 where it explicitly denotes preservation while in, not removal from. The preposition 'out of or from' (ek) lexically allows both motion-from and separation-within senses. Because both constructions are attested with the same verb in the Bible, the verse does not settle the timing question by lexicon alone.

The 'first' (proton) ordering of falling-away and revealing of the man of lawlessness before the Day of the Lord weighs against the church being removed before those events, but it speaks of the Day of the Lord rather than naming the gathering directly, so it informs without closing the question by itself.

Saints beheaded for refusing the beast and his mark must lexically have been on earth during the beast and mark era, supplying canon evidence that some believers go through the tribulation. A pre-tribulation (before-the-tribulation) reading distinguishes these as post-rapture converts under a separate program, which is a framework distinction, not a lexical one in the verse itself.

'Assembly or church' (ekklesia, Strong's G1577) occurs 20 times in Revelation, dense in chapters 1 to 3 (the seven letters) and once at 22:16, with zero occurrences in chapters 4 to 19. One reading lens sees this silence as the church being removed; another reads the term as locally tied to the seven local letters and notes that 'holy ones or saints' (hagioi), 'chosen ones' (eklektoi), and 'servant or bondservant' (doulos) vocabulary continues throughout. The lexicon supplies the distribution fact but does not rank these two inferences.

variants.note: The cited passages lie in Matthew and the Thessalonian epistles, outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM (a computer-assisted method for tracing textual variants) was not consulted. No variant unit in the bundle bears on the timing question. The minor variants visible in Matthew 24:30-31 (the article 'the' on 'trumpet' (salpingos), ordering of angels) do not affect the gathering vocabulary or the 'after' (meta) in 24:29.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the 'after the tribulation' (meta ten thlipsin) of Matthew 24:29 as fixing the appearing after the tribulation, and the shared 'trumpet' (salpinx), 'cloud' (nephele), 'gathering together' (episynagoge), 'coming or arrival' (parousia), and gathering of the chosen ones vocabulary across Matthew 24:30-31, 1 Corinthians 15:51-52, 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, 2 Thessalonians 2:1, and 2 Thessalonians 1:7 as describing one event. The Bible's single return-vocabulary ('coming or arrival' parousia, 'unveiling or revealing' apokalypsis, 'visible appearing' epiphaneia), always tied to visible coming and chosen-ones-gathering, gives unified footing without need to posit a second prior phase. 2 Thessalonians 1:7 promises relief to the afflicted at (en) the 'unveiling or revealing' (apokalypsis), not before it.

Reads 'we shall be caught up' (harpagesometha) in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as a distinct catching up of the church prior to the 'tribulation' (thlipsis), citing the temporal silence of the verb itself and the precedent uses of 'snatch or seize' (harpazo) for sudden rescue (Acts 8:39, 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, Revelation 12:5). Anchors a prior-removal promise in Revelation 3:10 'I will keep you out of the hour of trial' (tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou) and reads the absence of 'assembly or church' (ekklesia) in Revelation 4 to 19 as the church not present during those chapters' events. Distinguishes the 'last trumpet' (eschate salpinx) of 1 Corinthians 15:52 (church-age last trumpet) from the trumpet of Matthew 24:31 (a separate Israel-program trumpet).

Reads the gathering as occurring during the latter part of the seven-year period, after the falling-away and revealing of 2 Thessalonians 2:3 but before the climactic outpouring of divine wrath. Accepts the shared 'coming or arrival' (parousia) and 'trumpet' (salpinx) vocabulary as describing one 'snatching' (harpazo) event while distinguishing the 'tribulation' (thlipsis), which the church endures, from the 'wrath' (orge), which the church is kept from (1 Thessalonians 5:9). The lexicon permits this middle reading because 'tribulation' (thlipsis) and 'wrath' (orge) are different word-forms with distinct distributions.

Treats the 'coming or arrival' (parousia), the resurrection, the judgment, and the eternal state as one consummating event with no thousand-year gap, and reads the gathering of 1 Thessalonians 4 and Matthew 24 as one moment at the visible return. Agrees with post-tribulation (after-the-tribulation) reading on the unified lexical pattern of return-vocabulary and on Matthew 24:29 'after' (meta), while differing on the millennium question.

hermeneutics.notes: The competing readings turn on how 'snatch or seize' (harpazo), 'coming or arrival' (parousia), 'gathering together' (episynagoge), 'tribulation' (thlipsis), 'wrath' (orge), and 'keep out of' (tereo ek) relate as a system, not on any disputed word-form. The vocabulary is agreed, the sequencing model is not. The lexical pattern leans toward a unified coming, but the verb 'snatch or seize' (harpazo) and the 'keep out of' (tereo ek) construction supply genuine room for the two-stage reading.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The gathering of believers to Christ in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 occurs at, and is identical with, the visible return of Christ after the tribulation of Matthew 24:29, rather than a separate prior event.
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds a verdict by asserting there is no separate prior secret rapture. The phrase 'secret rapture' is itself a framework characterization, since 1 Thessalonians 4:16 describes a loud command, voice, and trumpet, not secrecy, so even pre-tribulation (before-the-tribulation) advocates do not describe their position as secret in that sense. The neutralized form asks the timing and unity question without presupposing the answer. The verdict below is derived on the original stem as supplied.

lay_summary: Three anchor passages supply the vocabulary. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 the Lord descends from heaven with a loud command, an archangel's voice, and the trumpet of God; the dead in Christ rise first, and the living are caught up, 'we shall be caught up' (harpagesometha), in clouds to meet Him in the air. In Matthew 24:29-31 the Son of Man appears immediately after the tribulation, 'after the tribulation' (meta ten thlipsin), on the clouds with a great trumpet, and His angels gather the chosen ones from the four winds. In 2 Thessalonians 2:1 Paul binds the coming, 'coming or arrival' (parousia), directly to our gathering to Him, 'gathering together' (episynagoge), the related-root noun to the gathering verb in Matthew. The same trumpet word also appears at 1 Corinthians 15:52, where the change of the living is dated at the last trumpet. Across the Bible the return is named by three nouns, parousia, apokalypsis (unveiling), and epiphaneia (visible appearing), all denoting the visible bodily coming. That single return-vocabulary supplies strong unified footing for reading 1 Thessalonians 4 and Matthew 24 as one event after the tribulation, and Matthew's 'after' (meta) makes the sequence explicit. Three lexical realities keep the question contested. First, the verb for being caught up, 'snatch or seize' (harpazo), is used in the Bible both for sudden divine rescue (Philip in Acts 8, Paul in 2 Corinthians 12, the child in Revelation 12) and for forcible seizure, and it carries no temporal marker (no word fixing when) relative to the tribulation. Second, Revelation 3:10, 'I will keep you out of the hour of trial' (tereso ek tes horas tou peirasmou), uses the exact same construction (tereo, 'keep', plus ek, 'out of') as John 17:15, where Jesus explicitly prays not for removal but for preservation while in. The same words have opposite spatial force in their two Bible occurrences. Third, ekklesia ('assembly or church') appears twenty times in Revelation but only in chapters 1 to 3 and at 22:16, with no occurrences in chapters 4 to 19. One reader sees a removal in that silence; another notes that hagioi ('saints') and eklektoi ('chosen ones') vocabulary continues throughout, and Revelation 20:4 describes saints who refused the beast and his mark, which by lexicon means they were on earth during that era. Because the Bible's words are agreed but the sequencing model is supplied by synthesis, the proposition lands as genuinely disputed.
